content: The establishment of regional offices, if necessary, will help achieve the first two milestones of the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030. Step 1: Governmental Commitment The first phase, conceptualization, aims to secure political commitment for a plan to enhance human resources for health (HRH) data using the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) framework. By 2020, the Ministry of Health should adopt the NHWA framework and initiate steps to coordinate an intersectoral health workforce agenda through a dedicated HRH unit. Key outputs include: Advocacy materials, such as briefs, brochures, and technical notes, to emphasize the critical role of the health workforce. A sustainable, long-term NHWA implementation plan initiated by the Ministry of Health. Possible tasks include: Appointing a lead official or unit within the Ministry of Health to oversee NHWA data reporting. Gathering NHWA resources, such as the NHWA Handbook and data platform, from WHO offices or headquarters. Engaging with WHO regional and country offices to facilitate the initial steps. Preparing an adoption plan in collaboration with relevant ministries and senior leaders, ensuring sufficient background information to justify the plan, such as World Health Assembly resolutions and the benefits of HRH planning. Step 2: Governance A multistakeholder, multisectoral working group will coordinate NHWA implementation and strengthen HRH data. This group will build on existing structures, such as HRH units, observatories, and committees, and include representatives from various organizations with expertise in communication and data. Key outputs include: Establishing a multisectoral coordination working group with representatives from ministries (e.g., Health, Employment, Finance, Education, Defense), national health institutes, legal bodies, and other stakeholders. Defining clear lines of responsibility and accountability for the working group and its members. Agreeing on key policy questions and establishing a secretariat to support legal frameworks and reporting documents. Possible tasks include: Mapping stakeholders to identify participants with the necessary skills for the working group. Organizing the first meeting to adopt terms of reference, governance mechanisms, and accountability structures. Nominating a secretariat to supervise activities and a technical working group to handle data-related tasks. Step 3: Scoping and Planning During this step, the technical working group will map available data and systems in the country and develop a plan for additional HRH data collection. Core indicators will be defined based on key policy questions, and data sources will be prioritized for accuracy, completeness, and efficiency. Key outputs include: A scoping analysis document detailing the current HRH situation, data gaps, and information sources. A cost analysis for the first year of NHWA implementation and a plan for a regular rolling budget. A list of indicators, roles, responsibilities, and data flows for updating and analyzing NHWA data. Possible tasks include: Conducting consultations with health bodies, academics, and economists to identify additional data sources. Investigating how to maintain, process, and integrate data from various sources, including IT compatibility and data exchange strategies. Preparing a business plan outlining funding, human resources, infrastructure, and technology needs. Step 4: This step involves assessing national regulations on data confidentiality, ownership, and exchange. Key outputs include: Formalizing legal aspects of data gathering and exchange, including anonymization and removal of sensitive information. Establishing standard operating procedures (SOPs) for data access, sharing, and breach mitigation. Possible tasks include: Identifying national bodies responsible for ethics, data confidentiality, and anonymization. Obtaining legal advice to align terms of reference with national regulations. Establishing SOPs for data dissemination and breach reporting. Step 5: Data Compilation and Analysis This step focuses on collecting and managing data from multiple sources to answer key policy questions and identify data gaps. The technical working group will define quality and eligibility criteria and harmonize data for NHWA use. Key outputs include: A process document describing data sources and flows, with metadata and legal requirements. A finalized list of data sources and quality standards for NHWA indicators. Possible tasks include: Conducting a quality assessment of data sources and identifying gaps. Supervising data collection through a network of focal points and centralizing aggregated data. Step 6: The technical working group will interpret findings and develop recommendations for decision-makers. Key outputs include: Political and technical validation of the NHWA process. Policy briefs and reports on HRH data quality, gaps, and improvement actions. Possible tasks include: Organizing national workshops or consultations to gather evidence and validate findings. Preparing a final report with recommendations for sustainable NHWA data collection and management. Step 7: Dissemination HRH information collected through NHWA will be disseminated to stakeholders and the public. A communication plan will guide the dissemination process, including the use of WHO platforms for international data sharing. Key outputs include: A report on the state of HRH in the country, with summaries for broad audiences. Policy briefs for decision-makers and peer-reviewed publications. Possible tasks include: Defining target audiences and key messages for dissemination. Monitoring the diffusion of messages and gathering feedback for future implementation. Step 8: Process Revision This step reviews the processes used to gather, interpret, and disseminate HRH information, identifying strengths and weaknesses to improve future implementation. The goal is to transition NHWA from an initial launch to a regular activity with a sustainable budget. Key outputs include: A strengthened HRH information system with improved interoperability. Recommendations for scaling up and sustaining NHWA activities. Possible tasks include: Evaluating the effectiveness of the NHWA process and identifying areas for improvement. Preparing a roadmap for the progressive and sustainable implementation of HRH data monitoring.
